en.html:
The voice behind the blind soothed me. I bowed to it.

Prince Haruhiro of Maidono, abbot of Hachimangu. My third audience with him. His standing was somewhere in the clouds; his way of talking came and sat beside you. By now this arrangement no longer confused me.

More than a week had passed since Enoshima. Wounds and exhaustion were nearly gone—Aoe's visit had made a small withdrawal from that recovery, admittedly. Still, nothing prevented me from giving His Highness the proper courtesies.

Probably nobody had been worried about my supply of courtesies. Nevertheless, the Chief, who had been studying me carefully, now looked away toward the prince's seat. He spoke one word, as though asking permission.

What could this be? The future, he said. On my side the future had not applied for any change.

Two enemies. Two allies.

I clamped my back teeth together and forced my eyes wide. Such a disgrace I had shown. All the malice in me, I turned inward.

Tired? Wah. And who has sanctioned this luxury for me?

With these hands I had put people beyond even feeling tired. What explanation would I give them? How thick had my face become, to let that weak little word slip out?

Unbelievable. Pathetic fellow.

...Or had the rattling already begun? Was this show of endurance nearly finished?

—See. Again I was entertaining myself with soft thoughts.

A fortress arrangement.

Shrines and temples gave the local people a refuge for their hearts. In older times some were equipped to take the rest of the person also, serving as fortified strongholds during war.

Nikko Toshogu was perhaps the best example. Famous for its Yomeimon gate, it was also, according to one account, the Tokugawa family's last fallback if trouble drove them out of Edo Castle.

Toshogu guarded the Tokugawa clan; Hachimangu was the Minamoto's tutelary shrine. Underground works came standard with fortresses. Their presence here need not send my eyebrows climbing.

The question I had carefully walked around all this time. Now the walking room was finished.

Who would do it?

Obvious. Painfully, insultingly obvious.

They were not asking my opinion.
They were asking my willingness.

Would these hands kill Moriuji Ashikaga?

My hands trembled on my knees. Small, disgraceful movements. I tried to hold them still; no cooperation. While the thought of murder remained in my head, the hands would not listen.

...I could understand. Agree also, I could.

The Lord General's death might turn history. If the prince steered matters well, a better future for Yamato might follow.

Now was the moment. I understood the prince's thinking. Probably he was right.

If right meant greater happiness for Yamato, then yes, he was surely right. That much I could admit.

But.
